items.title: How the quantum vacuum perturbs atoms, shrinks black holes and formed our galaxies
items.excerpt: From the microscopic structure of particles and atoms, to the fate of black holes and the large-scale structure of the universe, the quantum ‘vacuum’ plays a role.

items.title: How to be happy: Tips from the pioneers of well-being research
items.excerpt: When the pioneers of modern happiness research shared insights on living well, one research-backed theme kept emerging: the importance of other people.

items.title: Can planting trees on riverbanks save salmon rivers from global warming?
items.excerpt: As rivers warm, reforesting their banks could help Atlantic salmon. A new method makes it possible to identify priority areas.

items.title: Glowing ghoul or chemical tool? The toxic chemistry behind Victorian séances
items.excerpt: Our Halloween decors today are filled with spooky things that glow. But decades ago, that glow was often caused by toxic phosphorous.

items.title: New research finds frequent disease outbreaks in B.C. salmon farms, endangering wild salmon
items.excerpt: The study raises urgent questions about the federal government’s approach to regulating salmon farms.

items.title: Why using AI saves doctors time but won’t fix physician burnout
items.excerpt: AI can save physicians time, but time saved is not the same as burnout prevented. The fix is organizational.

items.title: Corporate ‘orbital data centre’ proposals are dangerous for humanity
items.excerpt: Orbital data centre proposals involve thousands of satellites, each one twice the size of the International Space Station.

items.title: Where does all the hardware go? The hidden environmental footprint of AI data centres
items.excerpt: Canada’s new Responsible Data Centre Development Principles fail to address computer hardware alongside water and electricity usage.

items.title: From Ukraine to the Middle East: How drones and AI are rewriting the rules of modern warfare
items.excerpt: While technology may set the boundaries of warfare, human choices ultimately determine how effective the technology is.

items.title: Why the ugly history of IQ testing matters for AI and education
items.excerpt: To figure out what AI may be understood as replacing, we need to examine intelligence as a historical and dangerous idea — rather than as a biological fact.

items.title: Data centres: Opposing them and developing them are not the only two choices
items.excerpt: The question is not whether Canada builds more data centres, but what it asks of them before they draw on public systems and local landscapes.

items.title: Are you a creature or a machine? How to live in ecological community in a time of AI
items.excerpt: As we are bombarded with apocalyptic headlines about the future of artificial intelligence, the writer, farmer and environmentalist Wendell Berry can help bring us back to our earthly community.

items.title: Canada could save millions by developing its own operating system instead of relying on Microsoft Windows
items.excerpt: A national, open-source operating system could help reduce Canada’s dependence on the U.S. while improving security and saving a surprising amount of money.

items.title: AI can predict intimate partner violence before survivors disclose. But should it?
items.excerpt: Technology that predicts when someone might experience intimate partner violence can undermine a survivor’s control over whether, when and how they share their abuse,

items.title: My own security system flagged me, a Black woman, as an animal
items.excerpt: As Ottawa seeks billions in international investment in advanced technology, bias cannot be a moral footnote.

items.title: How lessons from fisheries management could help us govern Earth’s orbital space
items.excerpt: Orbital space management organizations could help ensure that future generations live with stars above their heads, rather than constellations of debris.

items.title: Universities are making different choices about AI. How will they fit with their public missions?
items.excerpt: A scan of publicly documented AI initiatives at research-intensive universities suggests universities may need to invest more in teaching.

items.title: Canada’s settlement services are going digital. AI should support workers, not replace them
items.excerpt: AI can improve access to settlement services in Canada, but human expertise must remain central to complex, legal and sensitive newcomer needs.

items.title: Why ‘vertical farming’ is not a fix for our food system
items.excerpt: Growing plants indoors means replacing free sunlight with expensive, energy-intensive systems.

items.title: Eight ways to feed ourselves if rogue AI destroys modern agriculture
items.excerpt: if AI shut down the electricity grid, it would swiftly shut down agriculture. Without fuel, refrigeration, irrigation and fertilizers, we would all have to get creative in feeding ourselves.

items.title: Playful satire or weaponized play? Why White House video games are so problematic
items.excerpt: If the White House wanted to teach the public about ongoing social issues, it could have built video games for its website that consider the various challenges surrounding those issues.

items.title: Here’s how scientists aim to speed up drug development for treating new viruses
items.excerpt: Generating up to 100 times more antiviral drug candidates than was previously practical — in weeks rather than months or years — could improve the odds of finding a drug quickly when necessary.

items.title: Scientists predicted ‘Friday 13 November 2026’ will be ‘doomsday.’ Should you be worried?
items.excerpt: An article published in ‘Science’ in 1960 predicted that, thanks to ever-increasing growth, in the year 2026 the human population would approach infinity.

items.title: Alien life? Why the possibility of exoplanet LHS 1140b emitting helium gas is so exciting
items.excerpt: The exoplanet LHS 1140b may have a temperature that could allow for liquid water on its surface. Just possibly, it could support the existence of life.

items.title: How does a bird virus infect a person? Surprising findings from B.C.’s human case of H5N1 avian flu
items.excerpt: The human avian flu case in B.C. demonstrates there is much to learn about the complex factors that may result in a virus developing the ability to infect humans.

items.title: How NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will open a window into the Milky Way
items.excerpt: From supernovae in distant galaxies to the packed centre of the Milky Way, the new Roman telescope will help us see and understand the ever-changing cosmos.

items.title: Science that makes you laugh? Canadian engineers win Ig Nobel Technology Prize for 3D ‘necroprinting’ with mosquitoes
items.excerpt: The team printed a honeycomb and a Canadian maple leaf, both roughly the size of a single grain of sand.

items.title: Snack names influence how filling we imagine they will be — new research
items.excerpt: Most people are likely unaware of how the sounds of brand names affect them.

items.title: Psilocybin may help the brain recover from concussion, new study shows
items.excerpt: Psilocybin could be an unexpected avenue for treating an injury that currently has few options beyond rest and symptom management.

items.title: Making mental health chatbots more culturally sensitive won’t necessarily make them safer
items.excerpt: Canadians are turning to AI mental health chatbots for support. But what if the bot agrees with the beliefs that are keeping you unwell?

items.title: OpenAI may have solved the Navier-Stokes equation — but mathematics is more than $1 million trophy hunts
items.excerpt: Silicon Valley may end mathematical trophy hunting by making sport of it. But the modern mathematical landscape is so much broader than that.

items.title: Advertising is coming to AI chatbots — and it could influence the answers you get
items.excerpt: AI companies are turning to advertising to fund expensive systems. But commercial incentives could influence how answers are generated.

items.title: Russian team ‘misused’ Claude AI to train a killer drone on scraped Ukrainian war footage
items.excerpt: Visual footage — even that created by journalists and civilians to document conflict and hold nations accountable — can now become raw material for weapons development.

items.title: How bacteria hijack viruses to shuffle their own DNA
items.excerpt: Bacteria have transformed some viruses — now called gene-transfer agents — into a means of exchanging genetic material among themselves.

items.title: AI music lawsuits raise questions about American companies and Canadian arts
items.excerpt: A recent survey of working musicians in Canada points to a growing discontent about AI in music, and points to how we could gain a music industry that allows Canadian music to flourish.

items.title: Cyber attacks? Bioterrorism? To ‘Pace the Frontier’ of AI effectively, we must improve our anticipatory thinking
items.excerpt: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argues for slowing the pace of AI development globally. We must use this time to learn how to anticipate, and test for, future threats.

items.title: Sharing non‑consensual ‘deepfake’ porn in Canada is now a crime. The law still fails the victims
items.excerpt: Canada’s current framework treats deepfake-based sexual abuse as isolated criminal behaviour, when it is systematic gender-based violence.

items.title: An invisible AI watermark is coming to your messages. Your relationships may pay the price
items.excerpt: If checking each other’s messages for AI fingerprints becomes a habit, even casual communication may be marred with suspicion and doubt.

items.title: We designed a new way to build miniature fluidic devices to enable personalized cancer treatment
items.excerpt: The devices make tumour-on-a-chip technology easier and cheaper to build, with the hope they can be moved into clinical use for personalized cancer treatment.

items.title: The listening gap is real — how AI might help teachers bridge it
items.excerpt: The very tool that generates disinformation and slop could also, when used well, be a catalyst for teaching youth to listen.

items.title: AI agents can now remember and hackers can ‘poison’ their memories — a new cybersecurity threat
items.excerpt: Memory makes AI agents more useful, but it can also allow malicious instructions to remain hidden and influence decisions long after an attack.

items.title: Will AI save or ruin democracy? It depends on whether we allow computers to stand in for people
items.excerpt: Have we become trapped in thinking that better politics is just a technical fix away?

items.title: Ancient fossil from China reveals animal-microbe partnerships dating back 550 million years
items.excerpt: A sulfur-oxidizing bacteria may have turned a hostile environment into an ecological opportunity for the ancient conotubus organism.

items.title: Decoding Trump’s chaos: What science tells us about how Canada — and the world — should respond
items.excerpt: As uncertain as Donald Trump’s new world order is, science can explain the effects of his aggression and how to respond.

items.title: Why do we trust chatbots and how can we use them more wisely? A psychologist explains
items.excerpt: Research on language processing fluency can help us become aware of our psychological tendencies, and how to use them more productively with gen AI chatbots.

items.title: How AI-powered policing is endangering the public’s trust in police
items.excerpt: Growing concerns about police use of AI could erode the public’s perception of trust in the legal system.
